q6.answer: Each write inserts a row in the SoT database's outbox (users_sync_outbox in MySQL before the switch) in the same transaction as the write, so the record is durable and atomic with the commit, even if the app dies right after. The drainer worker polls the outbox, re-reads the current row from the SoT primary, applies it to Postgres with the version rule and tombstone guard, and deletes the outbox rows, retrying forever with backoff (it alerts after 5 minutes).

q7.answer: Delete inserts a tombstone (users_erased) and deletes the row in one transaction. Every copy statement (dual write, backfill, repair) has a NOT EXISTS tombstone guard, so a copy cannot re-create an erased id. The drainer also re-reads the SoT primary and, if the row is gone, writes the tombstone and deletes it on the follower. Tombstones are safe because MySQL does not reuse ids. I also wait 2 minutes after all instances dual-write so stale replica reads cannot miss a delete.

q8.answer: Progress is backfill_state.last_id in Postgres, updated in the same Postgres transaction as each batch upsert (UPDATE ... WHERE last_id < max id), so the cursor and copied rows commit atomically. A lease row prevents two runners. It stops when a read with id > last_id returns no rows; batches are 1,000 rows and it pauses while replica lag is over 5 s or missing.

q9.answer: A full comparison job walks both tables in id order and classifies each id as missing in Postgres, extra in Postgres, or different. It rechecks each against the MySQL primary and the outbox, and counts only persisting differences with no pending outbox row as mismatches. It heals each by inserting an outbox row, so the drainer fixes it (for an extra row, it tombstones and deletes it). A pass with any mismatch fails and is rerun until 0; equal version with different content pages a human. It reruns daily during the soaks.

q10.answer: Flags alone cannot do this because they lag up to 30 seconds across instances. So each database has a migration_fence row, and every user write takes a shared lock on the SoT fence and fails with a retryable 503 if it is closed. The switcher closes the MySQL fence (waiting for in-flight writes), drains, sets the Postgres sequence, opens the Postgres fence, then flips users.sot. Instances on a stale flag hit the closed fence and get 503 until they refresh, so no one writes MySQL-first after the close. A 45-second deadline covers the drain; if it is exceeded before the Postgres fence opens, the switch aborts and reopens the MySQL fence. A watchdog reopens it after 60 seconds if the script crashes. Worst case is 75 seconds, under 90.

q11.answer: Postgres assigns ids through a GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY column. At the switch its sequence is set to greatest(MySQL max(id), Postgres max(id)) + 1000, past every existing id. Before the switch, MySQL ids are inserted explicitly. On rollback, MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT is set to max(id) + 1000 before the MySQL fence opens, so MySQL also continues past all ids used in Postgres.

q12.answer: After the switch the same outbox mechanism runs in reverse (users.sot=pg, users.mirror=both): writes commit to Postgres with a Postgres outbox row, make a best-effort copy to MySQL, and the drainer repairs the rest with the version rule and tombstones. Rollback is a scripted write pause: close the Postgres fence, drain the Postgres outbox to zero, raise MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT, open the MySQL fence, and set sot=mysql with mirror=both. The option ends at step 11, no sooner than 14 days after the switch, when users.mirror=deletes_only stops copying creates and updates to MySQL. Dropping the MySQL table comes later, after a final dump.
